title: How the Browser Reaches a Server
summary: Follow a request as DNS finds the server's number, a port picks the program, HTTP carries the messages, and HTTPS keeps them private.
intro: When you press Enter, your browser knows only a name, like example.com. Before any page comes back, it has to turn that name into the number of a real computer, reach the right program on that computer, ask for the page in words the server understands, and keep the conversation private. Each of those steps can fail, and each failure has its own message: a site that can't be found, a server that refuses to answer, a 404, a warning that a site may not be who it says it is. This lesson walks through the steps in order, with a small server on your own computer and a few real sites, so that when a step fails, you'll know which one, and why.

steps.title: Names, numbers, and DNS
steps.body:
Computers on the internet find each other by number, not by name. Names are for people. So the first thing your browser does with an address is look up the number behind its name, and when that lookup fails, you get a message like This site can't be reached before any server has even been asked.

## IP addresses

Every computer on the internet has an **IP address**, a number that says where to deliver messages for it, the way a phone number says which phone to ring. IP stands for Internet Protocol, the basic rules every computer on the internet follows to send messages to the others. An address comes in one of two forms:

- **IPv4**, the original, is four numbers from 0 to 255 with dots between them, like `104.20.23.154`. There are only about 4.3 billion of them, fewer than the devices that want one.
- **IPv6**, the newer one, is much longer, like `2606:4700:10::6814:179a`: eight groups of digits and the letters a to f, where `::` stands for groups that are all zero. There are enough for every device that will ever exist.

Most sites have both, and your computer uses whichever its network supports.

## DNS, the internet's contacts list

Nobody wants to remember numbers like those, so sites have names, and a system turns each name into its number. That system is **DNS**, the Domain Name System. It works like the contacts list on your phone: you tap a name, and the phone looks up the number to dial. When someone registers a domain name like `example.com`, they also tell DNS which IP address it points to.

## The lookup

Asking DNS for a name's number is called a **lookup**. Keeping a copy of an answer to reuse later is called **caching**, and the copies are a **cache**. A lookup goes through a chain of caches, and it stops at the first one that already knows the answer:

- **Your browser** remembers names it looked up in the last few minutes.
- **Your operating system**, the software that runs everything else on your computer (macOS, Windows, or Linux), keeps a cache shared by every program.
- A **resolver** is a DNS server that does the asking for you. Your internet provider runs one, and public ones like `1.1.1.1` (from Cloudflare) and `8.8.8.8` (from Google) are free to use. Its cache is shared by everyone who uses it, so a popular name is almost always in it.

When nobody along the way knows, the resolver finds out itself, starting from the top of the tree of names:

```diagram dns-lookup
The resolver does the walking, and caches what it learns on the way.
```

In step 1, your browser asks the resolver for `example.com`. Names are read from the right, so in step 2 the resolver asks a **root server**, one of the servers at the very top of DNS. It doesn't know `example.com`, but it knows which servers handle every name ending in `.com`. In step 3, a `.com` server tells the resolver which server holds the records for `example.com`. In step 4, that domain's own **name server** gives the real answer. The resolver hands the address back to your browser, and keeps a copy.

## Records, and how long they last

A name server holds **records**, each one a fact about a name. Three kinds cover most of what you'll meet:

- An **A** record holds an IPv4 address: `example.com` is at `104.20.23.154`.
- An **AAAA** record holds an IPv6 address: `example.com` is at `2606:4700:10::6814:179a`.
- A **CNAME** record holds another name to look up instead: `developer.mozilla.org` is `mozilla.map.fastly.net`.

Every record comes with a **TTL**, its time to live, in seconds: how long any cache may keep it before asking again. A TTL of 300 means five minutes. Caching is what makes DNS fast, since most lookups never get past your computer or your resolver.

It's also why a change to DNS takes a while to reach everyone. When a site moves to a new server and changes its record, every cache that holds the old address keeps using it until its TTL runs out. People call this waiting for DNS to spread, but nothing spreads: old copies just expire, one cache at a time. Teams lower a record's TTL a day before a planned move, so the old answer dies out fast.

examples.title: Looking up a name with nslookup
examples.prompt: `nslookup` works in the terminal on a Mac, on Windows, and on Linux. The `1.1.1.1` at the end asks Cloudflare's public resolver, so your answer should match this one.
examples.output:
Server:		1.1.1.1
Address:	1.1.1.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:	example.com
Address: 172.66.147.243
Name:	example.com
Address: 104.20.23.154
examples.explanation: The first two lines name the resolver that answered. The `#53` after its address is the port DNS servers answer on, a number the next part explains. Leave the `1.1.1.1` off and nslookup asks your network's usual resolver instead, and prints that one's address here. Non-authoritative answer means the answer came from the resolver's cache, not straight from example.com's own name server. Then come the addresses: `example.com` has two, and a browser can use either one. Big sites list several, so visitors spread across their servers, and one server can fail without taking the site down.

examples.title: Following another name with dig
examples.prompt: `dig`, on macOS and Linux, shows more detail. `@1.1.1.1` picks the resolver, and `+nocmd +noall +answer` keeps only the answer. developer.mozilla.org is MDN, the reference site web developers use most.
examples.output:
developer.mozilla.org.	49	IN	CNAME	mozilla.map.fastly.net.
mozilla.map.fastly.net.	49	IN	A	151.101.129.91
mozilla.map.fastly.net.	49	IN	A	151.101.193.91
mozilla.map.fastly.net.	49	IN	A	151.101.1.91
mozilla.map.fastly.net.	49	IN	A	151.101.65.91
examples.explanation: Each line is one record: the name, its TTL in seconds, `IN` for internet, the kind of record, and its value. The names end in a dot, which stands for the root at the very top of the tree. The first record is a CNAME: `developer.mozilla.org` is another name for `mozilla.map.fastly.net`. Fastly is a company that keeps copies of sites on servers around the world and answers each visitor from one nearby. The resolver looked up that second name too, and returned its four A records in the same answer. Many big sites work this way: their name points at a company that serves them, and that company decides which servers answer. The TTL is how long the resolver will keep its copy, so run the command again and you'll see the number count down.

steps.title: Ports and localhost
steps.body:
An IP address finds a computer, but a computer runs many programs that use the network at once: your browser, a chat app, maybe a server or two. Something has to say which program each message is for, and that's the job of a port. You'll type ports every day as a web developer, since every server you run while you build has one.

## Ports

A **port** is a number from 0 to 65535 that picks one program on a computer. If the IP address is a building's street address, the port is the apartment number. A server **listens** on a port: it asks the operating system to hand it every message that arrives for that number.

Some numbers have a job everyone agrees on, so addresses can leave them out:

- **80** is for `http`, and **443** is for `https`. `https://example.com` means port 443 without saying it.
- **53** is for DNS, which is the `#53` nslookup prints after a resolver's address.
- Servers you run while you build use higher numbers that don't clash with those. **3000** is common for tools that run on Node.js, and Hack University itself uses it. **5173** is where Vite starts, which this course uses later, and **8000** and **8080** are popular too.

## localhost, your own computer

Every computer can send messages to itself. The address `127.0.0.1` is the **loopback** address: whatever you send there never leaves your computer, and comes straight back in as if it had arrived from outside. The name **localhost** means the same thing, and it works on every computer without asking DNS. Its IPv6 version is `::1`.

That's how you try out a server before anyone else can see it. Start it on your computer, open `http://localhost:8000`, and your browser and your server talk through loopback. The messages still go through ports and all the usual steps, so it behaves like the real thing.

```diagram ports-loopback
One computer, three ports: each address reaches a different program, or nothing.
```

In the diagram, the browser asks for three addresses on the same computer. Port 3000 reaches Hack University, and port 8000 reaches Python's small server, the one you can start in any folder with `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1`. Port 8001 reaches nothing, since no program listens there, so the attempt fails at once with **connection refused**. A connection is the line a browser opens to a program before it asks for anything, which the next part explains, and refused means the computer is there, but nobody answers at that number. When you see that message, the server you meant to reach isn't running, or it's on another port.

## Who can reach your server

A server also picks which of its computer's addresses it listens on, and that decides who can reach it.

- `127.0.0.1`, or `localhost`, means loopback alone. Only programs on the same computer can connect. That's what you want while you build, and it's what the `--bind 127.0.0.1` in Python's command does.
- `0.0.0.0` means every address the computer has, its Wi-Fi one included. Anyone on the same network can connect, like a phone on your Wi-Fi. Use it on purpose, when you want to check a page on your phone, and never by accident.

## Address already in use

Only one program can listen on a port at a time. Start a second server on a port that's taken, and the operating system refuses with address already in use. Usually an earlier copy is still running in another terminal. Stop it with Ctrl+C in that terminal, or start the new one on another port, like 8001. To find out what's holding a port on a Mac or on Linux, type:

```bash
lsof -i :8000
```

It prints a line for each program using the port, with the program's name and its PID, the number your computer gave that running program. On Windows, `netstat -ano | findstr :8000` shows the PID too.

## The origin

The scheme, the host, and the port of a URL together are called its **origin**. `https://shop.example.com/cart` and `https://shop.example.com/help` share one origin, since all three pieces match. `http://shop.example.com` has a different origin, with another scheme, and so do `https://api.example.com`, with another host, and `https://shop.example.com:8443`, with another port.

```diagram url-parts
The scheme, host, and port make the origin. The path and query string are what the request asks for.
```

The origin matters because your browser's safety rules are built on it. JavaScript on a page can freely read information from its own origin, but reading from another origin needs that origin's permission. That's what stops a page in one tab from reading your bank's page in another. The JavaScript lessons come back to this when your code starts fetching information.

examples.title: A port where nothing listens
examples.prompt: Ask for a page on port 8001, where no server is running.
examples.output: curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 8001 after 0 ms: Couldn't connect to server
examples.explanation: curl gives up at once. `Failed to connect to localhost port 8001` says it found the computer, your own, but couldn't open a connection on that port, and `after 0 ms` shows it didn't have to wait: your computer said no right away, since no program was listening there. A browser shows the same thing as This site can't be reached, with a note that localhost refused to connect. Either way, the fix is to start the server, or to use the port it's really on.

steps.title: Connections and HTTP messages
steps.body:
Once the browser has the address and the port, it opens a connection and asks for the page in HTTP, the web's own language. HTTP's messages are plain text you can read, and reading them is the quickest way to find out why a page or a form isn't doing what you expected.

## Opening a connection

Before it sends a word of its request, the browser opens a **connection** to the server: a two-way line that delivers every piece of a message, in order, and sends again any piece that gets lost on the way. The rules for this are called **TCP**, the Transmission Control Protocol. Opening a connection is like starting a phone call by checking the line, and it takes three messages, called the **three-way handshake**:

1. The browser sends `SYN`: can you hear me?
2. The server answers `SYN-ACK`: yes, and can you hear me?
3. The browser sends `ACK`: yes. The connection is open.

That's one trip to the server and back, called a **round trip**, before the request even starts. To a server on the other side of the world, a round trip can take a tenth of a second or more, so browsers keep connections open and send many requests through each one.

## HTTP

**HTTP**, the HyperText Transfer Protocol, is the set of rules for what the browser and the server say once they're connected. Hypertext is an old name for text with links in it. A request is a few lines of text, in this order:

1. The **request line**: a **method**, which says what kind of request it is, then the path, then the version of HTTP.
2. **Headers**, one per line, each a name, a colon, and a value: facts about the request.
3. A blank line, which says the headers are over.
4. Sometimes a **body**: information sent along with the request, like what you typed into a form.

A response has the same shape, with a **status line** in place of the request line: the version, the three-digit status code, and a few words saying what the code means.

```diagram http-message
A request and its response share one shape: a first line, headers, a blank line, and a body.
```

The `Host` header names the site, since one server often holds many sites and needs to know which one you mean. In a response, `Content-Type` says what kind of thing the body is, like `text/html` for a page, so the browser knows what to do with it. `Content-Length` says how many bytes the body has, so the other side knows where it ends.

## Methods

The method says what the request wants. Your browser sends GET whenever you open a page or follow a link. The others come from forms and from JavaScript.

| Method | What it asks | Safe | Idempotent |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | send me this | yes | yes |
| POST | take this new thing, or do this action | no | no |
| PUT | replace this with what I'm sending | no | yes |
| PATCH | change part of this | no | no |
| DELETE | remove this | no | yes |

A **safe** method only reads. It never changes anything on the server, so a browser can send it again whenever it likes. An **idempotent** method has the same effect whether it's sent once or five times. Deleting note 42 twice still leaves it deleted, but posting a new note twice makes two notes. That's why your browser asks before it sends a form again when you reload the page the form led to: sending a POST twice could order the same thing twice.

examples.title: Reading a whole exchange with curl
examples.prompt: With Python's server running in `my-site` on port 8000, run this from a second terminal. The `-v`, for verbose, makes curl print everything it sends and receives.
examples.output:
* Host localhost:8000 was resolved. * IPv6: ::1 * IPv4: 127.0.0.1 * Trying [::1]:8000... * connect to ::1 port 8000 from ::1 port 64002 failed: Connection refused * Trying 127.0.0.1:8000... * Connected to localhost (127.0.0.1) port 8000 > GET /about.html HTTP/1.1 > Host: localhost:8000 > User-Agent: curl/8.7.1 > Accept: */* > * Request completely sent off * HTTP 1.0, assume close after body < HTTP/1.0 200 OK < Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.13.6 < Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 20:19:24 GMT < Content-type: text/html < Content-Length: 98 < Last-Modified: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 20:07:14 GMT < About me

About me

I am learning how the web works.

* Closing connection
examples.explanation: curl marks each line by who wrote it. Lines starting with `*` are curl's own notes: `localhost` turned into two loopback addresses, the IPv6 one, `::1`, was refused, since the server listens on `127.0.0.1` alone, and the IPv4 one connected on port 8000. Lines starting with `>` are the request: the request line `GET /about.html HTTP/1.1`, three headers, and the blank line that ends them, with no body. `User-Agent` names the client, and `Accept: */*` says any kind of answer will do. Lines starting with `<` are the response: the status line, the headers, the blank line, and then the body, the file itself. Python's server speaks the older HTTP/1.0, so curl notes that the server will close the connection after the body instead of keeping it open.

steps.title: Status codes, headers, and cookies
steps.body:
Every response starts with a status code, and it's the first thing to check when something goes wrong: it tells you whether to fix your request or whether the server is the one that broke. Headers carry the rest of the story, and cookies are how a site remembers who you are from one request to the next. ## Status codes The first digit of a status code says what kind of answer it is: - **2xx, it worked.** `200 OK` is the everyday one. `201 Created` means something new was made, and `204 No Content` means it's done, with nothing to send back. - **3xx, look somewhere else.** `301 Moved Permanently` and `302 Found` send the browser to the address in the `Location` header, which it follows by itself. `304 Not Modified` means the copy you already have is still good. - **4xx, the request has a problem.** `400 Bad Request` means the server couldn't make sense of it, `401 Unauthorized` means you need to log in, `403 Forbidden` means you're logged in and still not allowed, `404 Not Found` means nothing is at that path, and `429 Too Many Requests` means slow down. - **5xx, the server failed.** `500 Internal Server Error` is a crash or a bug in the server's code, and `503 Service Unavailable` means the server is down or too busy right now. The split between 4xx and 5xx tells you where to look: a 4xx means change the request, and a 5xx means fix the server. ## Headers Headers are facts about a request or a response, a name and a value on each line. Their names don't care about capital letters, so `Content-Type` and `content-type` are the same header. These are the ones you'll meet most: | Header | Sent in | Says | |---|---|---| | `Host` | requests | which site you mean | | `User-Agent` | requests | which browser or program is asking | | `Accept` | requests | what kinds of answer the client can use | | `Content-Type` | both | what kind of thing the body is | | `Content-Length` | both | how many bytes the body has | | `Location` | responses | where to go instead, with a 3xx | | `Cache-Control` | responses | how long the browser may keep a copy | `Content-Type` matters more than it looks. Its value is a **media type**: `text/html` for a page, `text/css` for a stylesheet, `image/png` for a picture, and `application/json` for data that JavaScript reads. The browser decides what to do with a body by its media type, not by the extension in the path, so a stylesheet sent as `text/plain` is ignored and the page shows up without its styles. ## Stateless, with cookies for memory HTTP is **stateless**: each request stands alone, and the server doesn't remember the one before it. That keeps servers simple, since any one of a site's many servers can answer any request. But a shop still has to remember what's in your cart, and a site has to remember that you logged in. **Cookies** carry that memory. A cookie is a small piece of text, a name and a value, that a server asks the browser to keep. The server sends it in a `Set-Cookie` header, say in its answer to your login: ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html Set-Cookie: session=7f3a9c2e

Welcome back, Sam

``` From then on, the browser sends it back in a `Cookie` header with every request to that site: ```http GET /cart HTTP/1.1 Host: shop.example.com Cookie: session=7f3a9c2e ``` It works like the ticket a coat check gives you. The attendant doesn't remember your face, but the ticket says which coat is yours. Here `session=7f3a9c2e` is a random label the server made up for you, and the server keeps a note of who it belongs to. Each request still stands alone, but now it carries a reminder of who sent it. The JavaScript lessons cover cookies in full, along with the browser's other ways to store things.

examples.title: A path the server doesn't have
examples.prompt: With Python's server running in `my-site`, ask it for a page that isn't in the folder.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.0 404 File not found Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.13.6 Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 20:19:24 GMT Connection: close Content-Type: text/html;charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 335 Error response

Error response

Error code: 404

Message: File not found.

Error code explanation: 404 - Nothing matches the given URI.
examples.explanation: The status line says `404 File not found`. The words after the number are free for each server to choose, and only the number counts, so this is the same 404 Not Found as anywhere else. The server still sent a whole response: headers, and a body that's a small HTML page explaining the error, which is the Error response page a browser shows. A 404 is an answer, not a broken connection, and that's why many sites send a friendly page with theirs. Look at `Content-Type` too: `text/html;charset=utf-8` says the body is HTML, and `charset=utf-8` names how its letters are stored as bytes. UTF-8 is the standard way, and it covers every language.

steps.title: HTTPS keeps it private
steps.body:
Everything in the previous parts travels as plain text. Anyone along the way between you and the server, like someone on the same café Wi-Fi, the company that runs the network, or any of the computers that pass messages along, could read it, and could even change it. That's fine for trying things on your own computer, and not fine for a password or a card number. **HTTPS** fixes it: it's HTTP, sent inside a protected connection.

## What the protection gives you

The protection is called **TLS**, Transport Layer Security. Think of the difference between a postcard and a sealed letter with a signature you can check. TLS gives you three things:

- **Privacy.** The messages are **encrypted**: scrambled with a secret key that only your browser and the server have, so everyone in between sees gibberish. They can still see which site you're connecting to, but not what you send or get back.
- **No tampering.** If anyone changes a single byte along the way, the other side notices and drops the connection.
- **The right server.** Your browser checks that the server really is `example.com`, and not someone pretending to be it.

The first two would be worth little without the third. A private conversation with an impostor is still a conversation with an impostor.

## Certificates

The server proves who it is with a **certificate**: a small file that says which domain names it's for, the dates it's good between, and a key that lets the browser check the server's **signature**, a mark only the real server can make. It's signed by a **certificate authority**, or CA, an organization that checks a site really controls its domain before it signs. It works like a passport: you trust it because you trust the government that issued it, and that government checked who you are.

Your browser and your operating system come with a list of CAs they trust. When a server shows its certificate, the browser checks that a trusted CA signed it, that it hasn't expired, and that it names the host in the address bar. If any check fails, you see a full-page warning instead of the site, like Your connection is not private. When it's your own site, that warning usually means the certificate expired, or doesn't list the name you used.

Certificates are free from CAs like Let's Encrypt, and they renew themselves every few months, so a site has no reason to skip HTTPS. You'll also see **SSL** in tools and settings. It's TLS's old name.

## The handshake

Before any HTTP is sent, the browser and the server run a **TLS handshake** over the open connection. The browser says which kinds of encryption it supports, the server picks one and sends its certificate, and the two agree on keys that only they know. In TLS 1.3, the current version, that takes one round trip.

```diagram https-handshakes
Two round trips go by before the request can leave.
```

So a first visit to an HTTPS site takes three round trips before the page starts arriving. Step 1 connects with TCP, step 2 sets up the encryption, and step 3 is the request and its answer. That's one more reason browsers keep connections open: later requests on the same connection skip steps 1 and 2.

## HSTS

A site can still be reached through `http://` by mistake, when you type its name without a scheme or follow an old link. Sites handle that two ways. Their `http` address answers with a **redirect**, a 3xx response that sends the browser to the `https` address instead, and their `https` responses carry a header called **HSTS**, short for HTTP Strict Transport Security. Once your browser has seen it, it goes straight to HTTPS for that site by itself, for as long as the header says, and never tries plain HTTP first.

examples.title: What a TLS connection agreed on
examples.prompt: On a Mac or on Linux, connect to example.com and show only the lines about the connection. Everything after the address hides the page and keeps those lines, so you can type it as it is.
examples.code: curl -sv -o /dev/null https://example.com 2>&1 | grep -E "Connected to|ALPN|SSL connection|subject:|start date|expire date|issuer:|verify ok|using HTTP"
examples.output:
* Connected to example.com (2606:4700:10::6814:179a) port 443
* ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / AEAD-CHACHA20-POLY1305-SHA256 / [blank] / UNDEF
* ALPN: server accepted h2
*  subject: CN=example.com
*  start date: Sep 26 22:49:11 2026 GMT
*  expire date: Dec 25 22:56:35 2026 GMT
*  issuer: C=US; O=SSL Corporation; CN=Cloudflare TLS Issuing ECC CA 3
*  SSL certificate verify ok.
* using HTTP/2
examples.explanation: The first line shows the connection on port 443, the one for `https`. `ALPN` is how the two sides pick an HTTP version during the handshake: curl offers `h2`, which is HTTP/2, and `http/1.1`, and the server picks `h2`. The `SSL connection` line names the TLS version, 1.3, and the kind of encryption chosen. The certificate lines show its subject, the name it was issued for, the dates it's good between, and the CA that signed it, and `verify ok` means every check passed. This certificate lasts about three months, so it's replaced well before the end date. Your curl may print these lines a little differently, depending on how it was built.

examples.title: From http to https
examples.prompt: Ask GitHub for its plain `http` address. `-I` asks for the status line and headers alone. The second command, for a Mac or Linux, shows the HSTS header on the `https` side.
examples.code:
curl -I http://github.com
curl -sI https://github.com | grep -i strict-transport
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Content-Length: 0
Location: https://github.com/

strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includeSubdomains; preload
examples.explanation: The first answer is a `301 Moved Permanently` with a `Location` header pointing at `https://github.com/`, and no body, so `Content-Length` is 0. A browser follows it by itself, which is why typing an `http` address still lands you on the secure page. The second line is the HSTS header from the `https` site. `max-age=31536000` is one year in seconds: for that long, your browser won't even try plain `http` for GitHub. `includeSubdomains` stretches the rule to every name ending in github.com, and `preload` asks browsers to build the rule in, so even a first visit is protected.

steps.title: HTTP versions and the Network panel
steps.body:
When a page is slow, the first question is where the time went: finding the server, connecting, setting up encryption, waiting for the server, or downloading. Your browser can show you, and this part puts every step of the lesson on one timeline. First, a word on the versions of HTTP you'll see in those tools.

## HTTP versions

HTTP has been improved over the years, but its messages stay the same in every version: methods, paths, headers, status codes, and bodies. What changes is how they travel.

- **HTTP/1.1** (1997) sends text, one request at a time on each connection. To fetch many files at once, browsers open about six connections to each site.
- **HTTP/2** (2015) sends the same messages in a compact form that's faster for computers to read, and lets many requests and responses share one connection at the same time, so one slow file doesn't hold up the rest. Tools show its header names in lowercase.
- **HTTP/3** (2022) goes further and replaces TCP with newer rules called **QUIC**, which fold connecting and encrypting into a single round trip.

The browser and the server agree on a version during the TLS handshake, so you never pick one in an address, and the pages you write work the same in all three.

## The Network panel

The browser's DevTools, the developer tools built into every browser, have a **Network** panel that lists every request a page makes. To open it, press F12 (or Command, Option, and I on a Mac), choose the **Network** tab, and reload the page. Each row is one request, with its name, status code, type, size, and how long it took. A busy page can make a hundred or more, and a red row is one that failed.

Click a row to see that request's headers, then its **Timing** tab to see where the time went, split into the steps this lesson covered. Here's one request to example.com, drawn from the times in the example below:

```diagram request-timing
One request, split into the steps that make it up. Step 4 includes the server's own work.
```

1. **DNS lookup** is finding the IP address. It took 3 milliseconds, thousandths of a second, because the answer was already in a cache.
2. **Connect** is the TCP handshake, one round trip. Chrome calls it Initial connection.
3. **Secure** is the TLS handshake, another round trip plus checking the certificate. Chrome calls it SSL.
4. **Wait for server** is the request traveling there, the server working on its answer, and the first byte of the answer traveling back. The moment that first byte arrives is called the **time to first byte**.
5. **Download** is the rest of the response. This page is tiny, so it was nearly instant.

When a page is slow, this tells you which step to blame. A long lookup points at DNS. Long connect and secure steps mean the server is far away, or there are many new connections. A long wait means the server is slow to answer. A long download means the file is big. The course comes back to this panel when you make pages fast.

examples.title: Timing each step with curl
examples.prompt: curl can report the same times from the terminal. `-w` prints the timings when the request is done, and `-s -o /dev/null` hides everything else. On Windows, write `NUL` in place of `/dev/null`.
examples.output:
dns         0.003111s
connect     0.019380s
tls         0.044859s
first byte  0.069090s
total       0.069199s
examples.explanation: Each number is the time in seconds since curl started, so a step is the gap between two numbers. The lookup took about 3 milliseconds, since the answer was in a cache. The TCP connection took about 16 more, one round trip. TLS took about 25 more, its round trip plus checking the certificate. Then about 24 more went by before the first byte arrived: the request's trip there, the server's own work, and the trip back. The download added almost nothing, since the page is under a kilobyte. These are the numbers in the diagram above. Run it twice and they'll change a little, since every trip across the internet takes a slightly different time.

recap:
- An IP address is a computer's number, and DNS turns a name into it through a chain of caches that each keep answers for their TTL.
- A port picks one program on a computer: 443 for https, 80 for http, and numbers like 3000, 5173, and 8000 while you build.
- localhost and 127.0.0.1 mean your own computer, and a server on 0.0.0.0 can be reached from your whole network.
- The scheme, host, and port make a URL's origin, which the browser's safety rules are built on.
- TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake, and HTTP sends a request and gets a response over it.
- A request has a method, a path, headers, and sometimes a body, and a response has a status code, headers, and a body.
- A 4xx means fix the request and a 5xx means fix the server, and cookies give stateless HTTP a memory.
- HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS for privacy, no tampering, and a checked identity, which a certificate proves.
